name: The Black Poplar of Chante-Grillon

location.address: Parc Chantegrillon (Jardin Chante-Grillon), Allée Jean Benais, 33300 Bordeaux

verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 29714, Licence Ouverte)
transport: Bus stop Cite Chantecrit (lines 4/45/7), a few minutes walk; no direct tram stop
verify_notes: Largest-girth tree in Bordeaux's whole remarkable-tree register: 741cm circumference, three trunks fused near the base giving it a monumental, almost sculptural look. One of only seven trees in Bordeaux to carry the A.R.B.R.E.S. association's official 2012 label 'Arbre Remarquable de France' (confirmed on bordeaux.fr, which calls it the tallest tree in this particular garden). Historically black poplar bark and leaves were used in folk medicine for rheumatism. DISAGREEMENT: the register gives height 19m, while the city's own le-mag article states 31m ('record du jardin'); the register gives trunk diameter 236cm while the city article gives 'diametre du tronc principal' 320cm, plausibly because the article measures across the fused multi-trunk base rather than a single stem. Both figures are real published numbers, neither picked as a winner. No age given by either source; flagged for that gap, not for existence. Also protected under the city's own PLU (urban plan) as a classified site alongside its remarkable-tree status, a further signal of official recognition.

name: The Pecan of the Jardin Public

location.address: Jardin Public, Cours de Verdun, 33000 Bordeaux

verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 4600, Licence Ouverte)
access: Free, public park (Jardin Public, Bordeaux's main 18th-century public garden)
transport: Tram C, Jardin Public stop, at the park edge
verify_notes: The tallest tree in the Jardin Public at 38m (both the register and the city's own le-mag article give this exact height, an unusually clean match). One of Bordeaux's seven officially A.R.B.R.E.S.-labelled 'Arbres Remarquables de France' (2012). Pecan is native to the eastern/central United States and needs summer heat to ripen its nuts; unusual as a mature specimen this far into a European public garden rather than an orchard. Trunk diameter and circumference are close but not identical between sources (register: girth 421cm, diameter 134cm; city page: diameter 114cm, circumference 358-420cm range) which is expected variance in remeasurement rather than a real dispute, both land in the same band. No documented age from either source. Standing in the same small central lawn of the Jardin Public as several other candidate trees (ginkgo, chinaberry, magnolia), so this anchors a compact in-park walk.

name: The Kentucky Coffeetree of Parc Bordelais

location.address: Parc Bordelais, central lawn area, 33200 Bordeaux

verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 3401, Licence Ouverte)
access: Free, public park (Parc Bordelais); the tree itself sits behind a safety perimeter due to trunk cavities, viewable but not approachable at the trunk
transport: Tram D, Courbet stop, short walk into the park
verify_notes: Official Bordeaux city tree page (m.bordeaux.fr) states this Kentucky coffeetree is 'more than 130 years old' and dates from the park's creation (Parc Bordelais opened 1888), making it one of the park's oldest plantings. Rare species in France, one of only two Gymnocladus species worldwide (the other from China); the French name 'chicot' (stump) comes from its stark, sparsely-branched winter silhouette that can look dead even when healthy. Wood historically used for fence posts and railroad ties in North America; colonial settlers roasted the seeds as a coffee substitute (hence the name), though raw seeds/pods are toxic. Significant trunk cavities mean the city has fenced it off and prunes it regularly to limit branch weight; flagged so the story can be honest that visitors view this one from a short distance rather than standing beside the trunk. Girth 292cm, height 14m per the register; vigour recorded as FAIBLE (weak), consistent with an old tree under active arboricultural management rather than a death signal.

name: The Magnolia of Place Gambetta
verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 1241, Licence Ouverte)
access: Free, public square (Place Gambetta, fully reopened to pedestrians in 2021 after a renovation)
transport: Tram A or B, Gambetta stop, right at the square
verify_notes: One of two magnolias explicitly named as protected heritage in Place Gambetta's PSMV (Plan de Sauvegarde et de Mise en Valeur), the historic-centre conservation plan; local press (Rue89Bordeaux, 2015) and the metropole's own participation platform both describe the square's magnolias as 'centenaires' (century-old) and specifically preserved through the square's 2021 West 8/Sabine Haristoy renovation, which added over fifty new trees around the old ones rather than replacing them. Girth 358cm, height 17m per the register. Stands in one of Bordeaux's most central, most-used squares, a very different setting from the parks (a street-level plaza tree, easy to combine with the Jardin Public cluster roughly 1km away on foot). Age is qualitative ('centenary') from press description, not a measured ring count; flagged for that reason, not for existence.

name: The Ginkgo of the Jardin Public

location.address: Jardin Public, Cours de Verdun, 33000 Bordeaux

verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 4732, Licence Ouverte)

https://www.aquitaineonline.com/actualites-en-aquitaine/bordeaux-metropole/8424-bordeaux-les-arbres-mieux-proteges.html (confirms the city's citizen-sourced remarkable-tree census and PLU protection process that this register comes from)
verify_notes: French local name 'Arbre aux quarante ecus' (the forty-crown tree), from the story of a wealthy 18th-century Montpellier amateur who reportedly paid 40 ecus for his first ginkgo sapling when the species was a costly novelty newly arrived from China via the Netherlands and England. Girth 405cm, height 27m, crown spread 27m per the register; officially registered as REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE and separately classified under the city's PLU as a protected site. A local blog post (unebonnenouvelleparjour.com) independently describes a golden carpet of ginkgo leaves under a Jardin Public specimen each autumn, though it does not give exact coordinates so it corroborates the species-and-park pairing rather than confirming this precise tree; flagged for that reason rather than any doubt about existence. No documented age. Ginkgo is dioecious and this individual's sex (whether it drops the smelly fruit) is not recorded.

name: The Redwood Twins of Chante-Grillon

location.address: Parc Chantegrillon (Jardin Chante-Grillon), Allée Jean Benais, 33300 Bordeaux

verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 29755 and gid 29773, Licence Ouverte)
access: Free, public park (Parc Chantegrillon, city-managed, same small garden as the register-topping black poplar bdx_001)
transport: Bus stop Cite Chantecrit (lines 4/45/7), a few minutes walk; no direct tram stop
verify_notes: Register twins: two coast redwoods (gid 29755, girth 393cm; gid 29773, girth 390cm) standing roughly 10 metres apart in the same corner of Parc Chantegrillon, both individually flagged REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE and PLU-classified. Folded into one entry per the register-twins rule, since a visitor sees a pair rather than two separate destinations. Coast redwood is native to the Californian and southern Oregon coast and is not a naturally long-lived species this far from home without irrigation and mild winters, so a matched pair reaching this girth in Bordeaux's climate is itself the notable fact; almost certainly planted together as a deliberate pair given their proximity and near-identical size. Sits in the same officially A.R.B.R.E.S.-labelled garden as Bordeaux's largest-girth tree (bdx_001, the black poplar), reinforcing that this small park was curated for exactly this kind of specimen. Single-sourced beyond the register itself (no dedicated press piece on these two specifically found this pass), so flagged; existence is not in doubt given the register's own recent (2026-08-13) publishable-status filtering, which already excludes stumps and felled trees.

name: The Caucasian Elm of Parc Bordelais

location.address: Parc Bordelais, near the lake, 33200 Bordeaux

verified_sources: https://opendata.bordeaux-metropole.fr/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/ec_arbre_p/records?where=statut_patrimonial like "REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE" (Bordeaux Metropole tree register, gid 3928, Licence Ouverte)

https://lestetardsarboricoles.fr/wordpress/category/arbre-remarquable/zelkova/ (general note that Bordeaux zelkovas were historically grafted onto elm rootstock, visible at the base of some specimens)
access: Free, public park (Parc Bordelais, labelled a 'Jardin Remarquable' by the French Ministry of Culture in 2011)
transport: Tram D, Courbet stop, short walk into the park
verify_notes: Register's French name 'Faux Orme de Sibérie' is a folk name, not accurate: Zelkova carpinifolia is native to the Caucasus and northern Iran, not Siberia, and was introduced to France in the late 18th century by the botanist Andre Michaux after he saw it near the Caspian Sea (a Michaux-planted 1786 specimen still stands at the Jardin des Plantes in Paris). Girth 371cm, height 23m, sited by the park lake ('PB_Lac'). Officially REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE and PLU-classified. Vigueur recorded as FAIBLE (weak) in the register; the species is naturally resilient to Dutch elm disease even when branches decline, so weak vigour is not itself a death signal, but worth a photographer's note. No individual press piece found matching this exact specimen, so flagged; general park-level corroboration (the species' known presence and grafting history in Parc Bordelais) and the register's own recent publishable-status filter support existence.

name: The Black Locust of Parc Bordelais

transport: Tram D, Courbet stop, short walk into the park
verify_notes: FLAG FOR THE WRITER: the register lists a substantial 412cm girth (thicker than either Chante-Grillon redwood) but only 3m height, with vigueur recorded as FAIBLE. That combination reads as a tree that has been heavily pollarded, storm-broken or cut back hard rather than a data error in a single field, since girth and trunk_diameter_cm (131cm) agree with each other internally. No press piece or second source found this pass to explain the history behind the short stature; a photograph would settle it immediately (either a dramatic wide, low, veteran silhouette worth seeing precisely because of that shape, or grounds to hold it for photo-check before publishing prose that assumes a normal tree form). Officially REMARQUABLE_SYMBOLIQUE and PLU-classified regardless. Robinia pseudoacacia was introduced to France from North America in 1601 by Jean Robin, gardener to Henri IV, and the genus is named after him. Single-sourced beyond the register; flagged for both the sourcing gap and the physical anomaly.
